edge.title: The vendor who sends someone else
edge.setup: It is wedding and event season. You book a photographer, caterer or decorator and pay a large advance. The sales call promised the senior person, 'personal coverage' and a named team. The agreement you sign says only 'photography package'. On the day, assistants you have never met turn up and the person you paid is elsewhere.
edge.tell: The thing you were promised in conversation is missing from the paper you signed.
move: Before paying, get every promise written into the booking: who will attend in person, how many people, which hours, what is delivered and by when.
Pay in stages and keep the largest part until delivery, never the full amount upfront.
If the vendor will not write the promise down, treat that as your answer and book someone else.
If it goes wrong, keep the messages, receipts and the agreement, send a written complaint first, and then approach the consumer commission.
edge.why: Verbal promises are cheap for a seller to make and impossible for you to enforce. A vendor sells the senior name to win the booking and then delivers whatever is cheapest, and only the signed terms can be held against them. Writing a promise down costs an honest vendor nothing, which is why a vendor who resists it is telling you something.
edge.variants: Same shape: a contractor who promises a named supervisor, a coaching class that promises a particular teacher, a caterer who shows a tasting menu and serves another.

scenario.question: You are booking a photographer for a family wedding in December. The studio owner promises on the phone that he will shoot it himself with a four-person team, and asks for a 70% advance today to 'block the date'. The quotation he sends says only 'Premium wedding package, ₹1,40,000'. What do you do?

choices.text: Reply asking him to add to the quotation who will attend in person, team size, hours and delivery dates, and offer a smaller advance with the balance on delivery. Pay only once the written terms match the call.
Pay the 70% today. He sounded sincere and the date might go.
Pay, and screenshot his Instagram posts showing him shooting weddings as proof of what he offers.
Pay a smaller advance but leave the quotation as it is, since you will remind him nearer the date.

lens.name: Cost incidence
lens.one_line: Whoever writes the cheque is rarely who ends up paying.
lens.detail: A cost lands first on whoever is billed, then moves to whoever can't get out of the way: tenants, commuters, customers, taxpayers. Arguments about who 'pays' usually describe the first step only. To know what a cost means for you, follow it until it reaches someone with no alternative.
elsewhere: A property-tax rise that shows up months later in your rent.
'Free delivery' that is built into the menu price.
A fee charged to the shop that turns into a surcharge on your bill.
lens.test: If this cost went up tomorrow, whose price, fare or tax would change? That person is the one paying.
lens.today: Namma Metro's ridership rose 12% while its fare revenue jumped 50%, and its loss still widened to ₹1,717 crore, The Times of India reports. Revenue growing four times faster than riders means each trip is bringing in more, so the cost of running the system is landing on the people who have no cheaper way to cross the city. With the loss still widening, ask who closes that gap next: the rider's fare, the taxpayer, or both.

moved.what: Namma Metro ridership is up 12% and fare revenue up 50%, but the loss has widened to ₹1,717 crore, The Times of India reports.
moved.so_what: A widening loss keeps pressure on fares. If Metro is your daily commute, work out your monthly spend now so a future revision does not catch your budget off guard, and compare it with a bus pass or a mixed route.

moved.what: The Sensex fell 1,484 points and the Nifty closed at 25,349.65 on Monday, dragged down by bank stocks, BusinessLine reports.
moved.so_what: If you hold SIPs or index funds, a one-day fall is not a reason to stop them; stopping locks in the low. If you were waiting to put in a lump sum you had already set aside, a down day costs you nothing to use, but do not borrow to 'buy the dip'.

moved.what: The state government is raising the minimum site size in housing schemes to 30x40 feet, The Times of India reports.
moved.so_what: If you or your family are applying for a site in a government housing scheme, expect a bigger plot and a bigger price. Read the official notification for the final size and cost before paying any application or registration amount.

moved.what: The Karnataka High Court has held that contract appointees cannot be removed arbitrarily before their tenure ends, The Times of India reports.
moved.so_what: If you are on a fixed-term contract, keep your appointment order and any extension letters where you can find them. The tenure written on that paper is what you can hold an employer to.

moved.what: Bengaluru Jatre runs from 4 to 13 December with over 200 events and 500 folk artists across the city, including a Sunidhi Chauhan concert, The Indian Express and Deccan Chronicle report.
moved.so_what: Block a weekend evening now if you want to go. For any ticketed show, buy only through the channel the organisers announce, not a reseller link forwarded on WhatsApp.

carry_over.prompt: Your trading-app balance has grown and a small withdrawal worked, but now you must pay a 'verification fee' to unlock the rest for a deal closing tonight. What is the giveaway?
carry_over.answer: Your profit exists only on a screen run by the people asking for your next deposit, and getting money out needs another payment first.
